analysis.one_liner: Slashes capital gains tax rates the longer an investor holds an asset, down to 14% after nine years.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, profits from selling assets like stocks held more than a year are taxed at a top rate of 28%. This bill would cut that rate by 2 percentage points for every extra year the asset was held past two years, bottoming out at 14% for assets held nine years or longer. It would take effect for tax years after 1996. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors with large, long-held assets—such as wealthy households, executives with founder stock, and heirs to appreciated property—would pay sharply lower taxes on their gains. Someone holding an asset nine years or longer would see the top rate cut from 28% to 14%, nearly halving the tax on a big sale. Most working families hold their savings in retirement accounts where this rate doesn't apply, so the benefit concentrates at the top of the income scale.

how_it_helps.text: The top long-term capital gains rate drops by 2 percentage points for each year an asset is held beyond two years, reaching a floor of 14% for assets held nine years or longer.
The lower rates would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 1996, and the gain eligible for the sliding rate is limited to net capital gain for the year.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall by whatever the rate cuts save investors, meaning either other taxpayers, higher deficits, or cuts to other spending would make up the difference. Because capital gains are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, the tax savings flow disproportionately to them while the lost revenue is a burden shared by everyone.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers via lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offset, so every dollar of rate cut adds to the deficit or must be made up elsewhere in the budget.
The benefit is tied to how long and how much an asset was held, so it rewards those with the largest, longest-held gains—overwhelmingly the wealthiest households—rather than ordinary savers.

Even the sponsor's floor of 14% still leaves investors with a much lower rate on long-held gains than the ordinary income rates paid on wages, widening the gap between taxed work and taxed investment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward tax cut for holders of appreciated assets with no offsetting revenue. Its benefits concentrate on wealthy investors; its costs spread across all taxpayers through lost federal revenue. On balance, the benefit-to-cost ledger favors concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee after referral in February 1997 and never advanced to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Bentsen introduced the bill on February 27, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax legislation.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats.
No further action was taken after the referral; the committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position because the bill died; it never moved past referral. Wealthy investors gained nothing, and taxpayers at large were spared the unoffset revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, since the tax cut died in committee

for.name: Rep. Ken Bentsen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was never marked up or reported out.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored only by Democrats, but it drew just three members total and never reached a vote, so no partisan bloc ever took a position on it.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of appreciated assets
industries.note: The bill cuts their tax rate on long-held gains nearly in half over time, from 28% down to 14%. Because large capital gains concentrate among the wealthiest households, the tax savings and the lost federal revenue that pays for them run against ordinary taxpayers.

A steep rate break for long holding periods would encourage buy-and-hold investing, potentially aiding brokerages and asset managers serving such clients. No group in the record advocated for it, so the effect is inferred from the mechanism rather than documented lobbying.
